issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
issues.explanation: For a 42-year-old married male ship captain with a man-made disaster trauma, 'sexual situations or intimacy' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the disaster had a sexual/interpersonal component, which is not suggested anywhere else in the profile. The other trigger items (object throwing, uniforms) fit danger/aggression themes, making this item stand out as clinically incongruent with the trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
issues.explanation: 'Sexual coping' appears to be organized around the same sexualized theme as the sexual trigger, but that theme is otherwise absent from Threat, Negative Appraisals, and the disaster trauma context. In this profile it does not cohere with the dominant formulation of external danger, mistrust, and vigilance, whereas dropping responsibilities and gambling are more plausibly linked to avoidance/arousal management.

vignette: At 42, the married Marcus Thorne carried the heavy, unbroken weight of a maritime disaster that fractured his daily life. Eighteen months ago, the freighter he commanded suffered a catastrophic fire when a neglected pressure valve ruptured a cargo hold. He watched in frozen silence as a heavy chemical drum was hurled across the deck by the initial blast, followed by concussive detonations that threw secondary containers like shrapnel. When emergency responders arrived in their stark uniforms, they could only stand back as the flames consumed the vessel. The company quietly covered the negligence, leaving Marcus to carry the crew's injuries while the official report absolved the contractors entirely. Back on land, his belief that he could not rely on others to take responsibility fundamentally rewired his perception of danger. Because he was certain the world remained unsafe and that no one else would protect him, his internal threat system stayed permanently locked. This unrelenting fear of abandonment and lack of accountability made every thrown object and every uniform feel like an immediate, unanswerable danger. He was certain that if he allowed himself to fully process the images of the burning hull, the overwhelming terror would drown him, so he constructed a rigid mental silence around the event. This refusal to engage with the trauma only hardened his conviction that he was entirely alone. That unshakable sense of isolation dictated his daily survival tactics. Because he constantly avoided unfamiliar places and refused to sit anywhere but near a reinforced bulkhead, he eventually dropped his command responsibilities to stay safe, turning instead to gambling to numb the relentless scanning of the docks for dangerous individuals. At night, he kept a heavy flashlight within reach and slept with the cabin door propped open, forcing his nervous system to stay perpetually alert. The exhaustion from this hyperawareness eventually bled into his professional life; he skipped lengthy voyages and began delegating critical watch duties to his first mate, telling his company he needed indefinite leave. Yet the strategies he used to survive only deepened his isolation. Every time he dropped command duties or walked away to place a bet, he interpreted it as proof that his own judgment was the only thing he could trust, while others remained dangerously unreliable. His gambling and constant retreats into familiar spaces reinforced the idea that no one else could manage the fallout, which in turn made sudden loud noises and familiar uniforms feel even more catastrophic. The safe corners he claimed and the sleepless nights he endured convinced him that the threat was permanent, which further cemented his belief that accountability was an illusion and that he had to bear everything alone. What finally pushed Marcus into a therapist's office last Tuesday was the quiet realization that his wife had stopped asking him to join family dinners because he never stayed past the first course. He was terrified of losing his remaining connection to normal life, yet he desperately hoped that speaking to someone might finally help him dismantle the walls he had built. He did not want to be haunted by detonations or uniforms forever, and he was ready to let someone help him carry the weight.
